meta.title: Working With LLMs
meta.mystery: Why do experienced AI users get dramatically better results from the same model?

arrive.title: Two designers. One model.
arrive.subhead: Same AI. Same request. Watch what happens.

predict.title: “Design our new landing page.”
predict.subhead: Designer A opens a brand-new chat. Designer B opens one organized project – brand notes, a style sample, past decisions, pinned instructions. Both type the exact same sentence.
predict.predictionPrompt: How different will the two results be?

reveal.title: Same model. Same sentence. Not the same result.

designerA.body: A generic page. “Welcome to our company.” Stock structure. Could belong to anyone.

designerB.body: On-brand voice. The audience it’s for. A layout that echoes decisions the team already made. Reads like a teammate wrote it.

reveal.surpriseLine: The model was identical. Only what surrounded the request changed.

inspect.title: Look closer.
inspect.subhead: Designer B’s project isn’t a better AI. It’s the same AI with more around it.
inspect.workspaceA: Empty chat – one sentence, nothing else.
inspect.workspaceB: Same sentence + brand notes, audience, a style sample, past decisions, pinned do’s and don’ts.

pick.title: What actually produced the better page?

reveal.title: It wasn’t the model. It wasn’t clever wording.
reveal.body1: The model never changed. Designer B didn’t write a longer sentence – they wrote the same one.
reveal.body2: What changed was the context: everything the model could see when it answered. Brand notes, audience, examples, past decisions. That’s the difference between “anyone’s page” and “your page.”
reveal.punchline: Beginners polish the prompt. Experienced users build the context.

recall.title: Remember what the model actually does.
recall.subhead: From the training room: it predicts its next words – one at a time – based on everything in front of it.
recall.body: Context is that “everything in front of it.” Change what it can see, and you change what it predicts. You’re not making it smarter. You’re aiming it.

toggle.title: Same request. Flip one thing at a time.
toggle.subhead: Turn each piece of context on or off and watch the answer move.
toggle.helperAllOff: With nothing to condition on, the model falls back on the average of everything it ever learned. That’s why it sounds generic.
toggle.helperAllOn: Now every prediction is steered by your world – not the internet’s average.
toggle.genericAnswer: Welcome to our company. We offer innovative solutions for modern businesses.

audience.label: Audience
audience.effect: Speaks to the people you named – not “everyone.”

brand-voice.label: Brand voice
brand-voice.effect: Sounds like your brand, not a stock template.

past-decision.label: Past decision
past-decision.effect: Respects a choice the team already made.

worked-example.label: Worked example
worked-example.effect: Echoes the shape of work that already succeeded.

scenario.title: You run a small bakery.
scenario.subhead: You use AI most weeks – captions, replies, menu text. Right now you re-explain yourself every time. Let’s fix that once.

assemble.title: Pin what the AI should always know.
assemble.subhead: Drag each card onto the board. This is the setup experienced users do once and reuse for months.

business.label: Business
business.body: Small neighborhood bakery, six years old, known for sourdough.

audience.label: Audience
audience.body: Local regulars and weekend walk-ins. Warm, not corporate.

tone-sample.label: Tone sample
tone-sample.body: Morning’s quiet until the first loaf cracks open. Come by for the sourdough – we’ll save you the corner seat if we can.

past-decision.label: Past decision
past-decision.body: We don’t discount. We add value instead.

do-dont.label: Do / Don’t
do-dont.body: Do mention daily specials. Don’t use exclamation-point hype.

compare.title: “Write this week’s Instagram caption.”

bare.body: “Check out our fresh baked goods today! 🥐 Come visit us!” – generic, hype-y, could be any bakery.

built.body: Names the sourdough, speaks to regulars, skips the hype, mentions today’s special – in your voice.

compare.surpriseLine: Same request. You just didn’t have to explain yourself to get there.

habit.title: “Write my launch email.” Send. Copy. Paste. Done.
habit.subhead: Most people take the first draft. Experienced users almost never do.

choose.title: The first draft lands. Now what?

approaches.critique: Ask it to critique itself – “What are the weakest parts of this?”

reveal.title: The critique pass changed the email.
reveal.body1: Asked for its own weak points, the model flagged a buried call-to-action and a vague opening – then fixed them.
reveal.body2: Nothing mystical happened. Your follow-up became new context, and the next prediction was steered by it. Each pass adds information; each answer gets sharper.
reveal.punchline: You’re not chatting with a colleague. You’re steering a prediction engine – and steering beats accepting.

street-sign.scenario: Translate one street sign while traveling
street-sign.note: One-off, no future use. Context is overhead you’ll never reuse.

company-style.scenario: Keep your company’s style consistent across a year of posts
company-style.note: Same voice, again and again – pin it once.

movie-year.scenario: Ask what year a movie came out
movie-year.note: A fact, not a relationship. Nothing to reuse.

weekly-reports.scenario: Draft weekly reports for the same project for months
weekly-reports.note: Recurring task, stable background – ideal for a project.

word-meaning.scenario: Settle a quick disagreement about a word’s meaning

personal-voice.scenario: Write in your personal voice across everything you do
personal-voice.note: Your voice is stable context worth saving once.

random-article.scenario: Summarize a random article you’ll never revisit
random-article.note: No follow-on work; a project adds friction, not value.

score.title: {score} of {total} matched the usual call.
score.subhead: Not everything deserves a project. The skill is knowing which is which.

task.title: How much should you spell out?
task.subhead: The task: “Help me write a cover letter for a marketing role.” Three people prompt it three ways.

pick.title: Which one gets the best result?

sweet-spot.label: Goal + constraints + success criteria
sweet-spot.detail: “Cover letter for a junior marketing role at a small agency. Warm but professional, under 300 words, highlight my events experience. Success = they can picture me on the team.”

micromanaged.label: Micromanaged
micromanaged.detail: a 20-step script dictating every sentence, transition, and word count per paragraph.

reveal.title: Both extremes lose. The middle wins.
reveal.body1: Too vague, and the model fills the gaps with the internet’s average – generic. Micromanaged, and you’ve done the thinking yourself and boxed it in – you get a worse version of your own outline.
reveal.body2: The winner names the destination and the constraints – role, tone, length, what to feature, what “good” looks like – and leaves the how to the model.
reveal.punchline: Be specific about where you’re going. Don’t script every step of the walk.

reflection.title: Complete the sentence.
reflection.subhead: No quiz. Just notice how your definition of “using AI well” shifted.
reflection.beforeLabel: Before today I thought better results came from…
reflection.beforePlaceholder: better prompts… magic words… the right model…
reflection.afterLabel: Now I think better results come from…
reflection.afterPlaceholder: better context… iteration… setup I reuse…

line.title: Beginners optimize prompts. Experts optimize environments.
line.subhead: Same model, in everyone’s hands. The difference is what you build around it.

oldHabit.body: Perfect the wording of one message.

newHabit.body: Build context once. Reuse it. Iterate on the answer.

principle.title: The buttons will keep changing.
principle.body: Projects, memory, workspaces, whatever ships next quarter – those are implementations. The principle underneath doesn’t move: context you build together beats wording you perfect alone. That’s true in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and whatever comes after them.

mystery.headline: If context is this powerful…
mystery.followUp: what happens when there’s too much of it – does the model weigh every word equally?

seoSpine.h1: How Do Large Language Models Actually Work?
seoSpine.lead: A large language model generates text by predicting likely next tokens from context. That is the shared mechanism behind tools people call ChatGPT-style assistants — and why clear context changes what you get.

sections.heading: What are tokens in AI?
sections.body: Models don’t always read whole words the way people do. Text is split into tokens — pieces of words or characters — and the model works over that sequence when it predicts what should come next.

sections.heading: How does an LLM generate text?
sections.body: Generation is repeated next-token prediction: given the tokens so far, choose a likely continuation, append it, and continue. How you frame the task — goals, constraints, and context — shapes those predictions.

sections.heading: Same model, different results
sections.body: Experienced users often get better outcomes from the same LLM by specifying the job clearly and iterating — not by assuming the model already knows what they mean.
